Some important things to understand about market structure:
-fundamentally nothing has changed since 10/10 re: alts and arguably has gotten worse
-as such, liquid funds can’t size as big on alt allocations. This was the main structural bid on “quality alts” in the past. Most people are just trading momentum/trend
-Capital / margin is more spread out because of the growth of cross-marginable stock / RWA perps. Fiat stables haven’t grown their market cap in some time now
-leakage: Hacks, exchange fees, launchpads, grifters. Same as before but recent uptick in hacks due to AI cyber capabilities 
-so who has money? (1) Basis/systematic traders who got favorably ADL’d on 10/10 ie not a source of bid on market beta (2) HYPE airdrop recipients/holders, who are mostly losing traders / momentum types (3) hackers who sell coins -> fiat

These aspects all contribute to crypto trading like absolute garbage outside of some short periods where people are forced to chase aggressively trending coins

The event calendar and ongoing risks look much different over the next four weeks than they did going into the previous four weeks. This move is getting long in the tooth and I think it's more likely than not that Waller's speech + today's CPI has provided an attractive opportunity to flip from a short to a long risk bias into next week's Anthropic IPO and possibly longer, TBD. This is not an all clear of the structural problems that exist, but a local call that the path to the final destination will not be easy nor in a straight line.

I wouldn't characterize the state of enterprise AI adoption this way. Broadly, I would say there are two variables in measuring the ROI of AI in an organization: 
1. The task you are automating or augmenting 
2. Does this business have any fucking idea why they are successful? 

#1 The task. 
Let's take a very simple example. Closing out a support ticket from a customer. Most companies know how much this costs by channel - say, $40 to pick up the phone, $15 to answer it by email, $5 by chat. This is calculating using things like the agent salaries, the headcount that supports them, the technology they use, the facilities, and any travel and training expenses

Now imagine you can use AI to *successfully* answer a question and the AI company you use charges you 70 cents for that. OK, you really clearly know the ROI of AI in this specific, bounded, use case.

Consider other tasks. The velocity with which you ship new products. A bit fuzzier but not a crazy task to determine whether 1) Developer productivity has increased 2) Whether that is bending the slope of your revenue curve upward.

Farther out on the curve. Being able to now generate 21 different versions of a marketing campaign's creative using your brand design assets. Making 40% of analytics requests self-service instead of being stuck in a queue for humans to answer. Quite a bit messier to measure direct ROI.

#2 Does the company have it's shit together? 

Do they know what is actually driving the business forward? I think that the answer for many businesses is actually, No. Do they reliably know who their top performers are? Do they know the actual 2-3 inputs that drive revenue growth? Not only do they know them but can they accelerate them? If you asked 10 people at the company what "the most important thing" was for the business, would they give the same answer? Again, I think the answer is mostly No. 

If you do not deeply understand your business, what is driving it, and who is driving it, it is quite hard to know whether AI is helping you. 
----------
TL;DR. For some tasks it is quite easy to measure the ROI. For others, less so. For some businesses who have their shit together, it is quite easy to measure the ROI. For others, less so.

First, equity and the broader liquidity era as we know it is just so over. ZIRP is a thing of the past. 2026 has been an echo bubble. We are in a permanent high rates regime now. Capital is scarce

Second, in spite of this, I can't help feeling bullish digital assets. I have questioned my own stance on this multiple times, it seems like some sort of cognitive dissonance. But I think it one of the factors it comes down to is valuation

Digital assets where they are today, are, for the most part, extremely cheap compared to stocks and showing rapid growth. Now, people still want to make returns on capital. But the hurdle is far higher in these environments. As a result, you really only want to invest in strong companies.

Digital assets have a natural discount on the basis of having 1) supply come online every month, 2) lack of regulation and investor rights, and 3) no real future expectation of growth in an arena full of rugs, scams, and stage-left exits

If you were to ask me, gun to head, how I would allocate the portfolio of tomorrow, with no cash positions at all, optimizing purely for returns, i.e a portfolio with the most amount of torque and venture-like outcomes

it'd probably be something like:

33% digital-altcoins

33% AI-adjacent winners - software / robotics / bio / etc.

33% frontier tech - quantum / space / etc. 

That being said, these high risk assets are the first to go in these regimes. Sizing is key in these moments. Not too large at the beginning, yet not too small.

First, equity and the broader liquidity era as we know it is just so over. ZIRP is a thing of the past. 2026 has been an echo bubble. We are in a permanent high rates regime now. Capital is scarce

Second, in spite of this, I can't help feeling bullish digital assets. I have questioned my own stance on this multiple times, it seems like some sort of cognitive dissonance. But I think it one of the factors it comes down to is valuation

Digital assets where they are today, are, for the most part, extremely cheap compared to stocks and showing rapid growth. Now, people still want to make returns on capital. But the hurdle is far higher in these environments. As a result, you really only want to invest in strong companies.

Digital assets have a natural discount on the basis of having 1) supply come online every month, 2) lack of regulation and investor rights, and 3) no real future expectation of growth in an arena full of rugs, scams, and stage-left exits

If you were to ask me, gun to head, how I would allocate the portfolio of tomorrow, with no cash positions at all, optimizing purely for returns, i.e a portfolio with the most amount of torque and venture-like outcomes

it'd probably be something like:

33% digital-altcoins

33% AI-adjacent winners - software / robotics / bio / etc.

33% frontier tech - quantum / space / etc. 

That being said, these high risk assets are the first to go in these regimes. Sizing is key in these moments. Not too large at the beginning, yet not too small.
